question.text: Which of the following diagrams depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown above?
question.explanation:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation.

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

\[ \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \]

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

example.title: Identifying the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Curve Using a Diagram

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $x_1^2-2x_1x_2+ x_2^2= 6?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+ x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1 - \lambda & -1 \\ -1 & 1 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 -2 \lambda &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 2, \, 0 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $2y_1^2 .$

In the new variables, the given curve has the following equation:

\begin{align*} 2y_1^2 &= 6 \\[3pt] y_1^2 &= 3 \\[3pt] \end{align*} This represents the two parallel lines $y_1 = \sqrt3$ and $y_1 = -\sqrt3.$

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $3x_1^2+10x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 32?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=3x_1^2+10x_1x_2+3x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 5& 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 3 - \lambda & 5 \\ 5 & 3 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 -6 \lambda -16 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 8, \, -2 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $8y_1^2 -2 y_2^2.$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

\[ \begin{align*} 8y_1^2 -2 y_2^2 &= 32 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{4} - \dfrac{y_2^2}{16} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{2^2} - \dfrac{y_2^2}{4^2} &= 1 \end{align*} \]

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $2$ and $4.$

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $9x_1^2+4x_1x_2+6x_2^2 = 10?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=9x_1^2+4x_1x_2+6x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 9 - \lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 6 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 -15 \lambda +50 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 5, \, 10 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $5y_1^2 +10 y_2^2.$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

\[ \begin{align*} 5y_1^2 +10 y_2^2 &= 10 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{2} + \dfrac{y_2^2}{1} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{(\sqrt{2})^2} + \dfrac{y_2^2}{1} &= 1 \end{align*} \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $1.$

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $5x_1^2+2x_1x_2+5x_2^2= 12?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=5x_1^2+2x_1x_2+5x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 5 - \lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 5 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 -10 \lambda +24 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 6, \, 4 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $6y_1^2 + 4y_2^2.$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

\[ \begin{align*} 6y_1^2 +4 y_2^2 &= 12 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{2} + \dfrac{y_2^2}{3} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{(\sqrt2)^2} + \dfrac{y_2^2}{(\sqrt{3})^2} &= 1 \end{align*} \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{3}.$

question.text: Which curve is defined by the equation $24x_1^2+4x_1x_2+21x_2^2 =100?$
question.explanation:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=24x_1^2+4x_1x_2+21x_2^2.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 2 \\ 2& 21 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A - \lambda I | &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 24 - \lambda & 2\\ 2& 21 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda^2 -45 \lambda +500 &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 25, \, 20 \end{align*}

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $25y_1^2 +20 y_2^2.$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

\[ \begin{align*} 25y_1^2 +20 y_2^2 &= 100 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{4} +\dfrac{y_2^2}{5} &= 1 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y_1^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y_2^2}{(\sqrt5)^2} &= 1 \end{align*} \]

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $\sqrt{5}.$

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 11.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-5,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 11 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 3 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-5) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -4 \end{bmatrix} + 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-5)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 5.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=10$ and $\lambda_2=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 5 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-3) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix} + 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=9$ and $\lambda_2=4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=9,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 9 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} -9 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=4,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 4I &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 7 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-4,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-4) I &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} + 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$ and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-7,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
question.explanation:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 3 \]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 3 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} - 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-7,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-7) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} + 7 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-7)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $5x_1^2+24x_1x_2-5x_2^2 = 52.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=5x_1^2+24x_1x_2-5x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 52 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=13 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-13.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=13,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 13 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5 \end{bmatrix} - 13 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 12 \\ 12 & -18 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-13,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-13) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 12 \\ 12 & -5 \end{bmatrix} +13 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 12 \\ 12 & 8 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $24x_1^2+4x_1x_2+21x_2^2 = 100.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=24x_1^2+4x_1x_2+21x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 100 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=25 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=20.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=25,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 25 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 2\\ 2 & 21 \end{bmatrix} - 25 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-25I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=20,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 20 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21 \end{bmatrix} - 20 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. %= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

example.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $7x_1^2+8x_1x_2-8x_2^2 = 9.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=7x_1^2+8x_1x_2-8x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 9 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=8 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-9.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=8,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 8 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8 \end{bmatrix} - 8 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-8I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-9,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-9) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 4 \\ 4 & -8 \end{bmatrix} + 9 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A+9I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $2x_1^2-4x_1x_2+2x_2^2 = 9.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-4x_1x_2+2x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 9 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=4 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=4,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 4 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

question.text: Find the principal axes of the curve $14x_1^2-6x_1x_2+6x_2^2 = 15.$
question.explanation:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=14x_1^2-6x_1x_2+6x_2^2.$ The matrix of the form is

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

\[ \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 15 \]

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I| = 0,$ we obtain

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=15 \quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=5.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

  • For $\lambda_1=15,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 15 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 15 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-15I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.$
